title: Bali keeps his word
hook: warned it's a trap, a king keeps his word anyway
carry: satya: a word given is a word kept
tomorrow: the water touches the ground. how big does the small boy get?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy asked for three steps, and said if three won't do, the world won't either: santosha, enough is a practice. Bali said yes. Then someone at his side spoke up.

Somebody always says it right before a signature: wait, don't sign that. Bali's teacher, Shukra, leans close at the sacrifice. That boy is Vishnu, he says. Those three steps will take everything you have. Take the promise back. The water for the gift is already in Bali's hand. And Bali doesn't take it back.
screen: `WAIT. DON'T SIGN THAT.` → `THAT BOY IS VISHNU.` → `THE WATER IS IN HIS HAND.`

segments.voice: Shukra makes a good case. A promise that would ruin you, he says, can be set aside, and no one would blame you. Bali answers with a line the Purana keeps: the earth can carry any weight except a person who lies. He's Prahlada's grandson, and if this really is Vishnu asking, what is there to lose? Shukra curses him for it. Bali pours the water anyway, and the gift is made. That water matters. In Hindu rites a gift or a vow is sealed with water, and you can still see it: at the start of a puja, many Hindus hold a little water in the right palm, say what they're offering and why, and let it go. It's called sankalpa, the resolve. Once it's poured, it's given. Bali is honored for that: satya, truth to your word. Now the week in one breath. The Lord lives in every being, said a child in a demon's palace. He stepped out of a stone pillar to keep his devotee's word. Bhakti at its height asks for nothing, and every asker is still welcome. The fierce god's hand on a child's head is a blessing. A vow offers what you can't fix. Santosha: enough is a practice. And Prahlada's grandson pours the water.
screen: `A RUINOUS PROMISE CAN BREAK?` · `THE EARTH CAN'T CARRY A LIAR.` · `SANKALPA: SEALED WITH WATER.` · `SATYA: A WORD KEPT.`

segments.voice: If you pray, hold a little water in your right palm, or just cup the hand, and say one promise you mean to keep, small or large. Then let the water go, or open the hand, the way Bali poured. Breathe with it for the sit. If it feels heavy, let each breath out carry a little of the weight.
Vamana: the small form of Vishnu, and the king who was warned who he was, and gave anyway.
The line: satya, a word given is a word kept. Bali poured the water anyway. That's the week.

howItsDone: Many Hindus begin a puja with a sankalpa, holding water in the palm while stating the offering, then releasing it. The Bhagavata Purana tells Vamana's story at length, and in Kerala the festival of Onam is kept in memory of King Bali, known there as Mahabali.
